notes.86.3: 94.4: 'ez streit abin' read as 'won by fighting from them'. 98.4: 'die kameren gewan' read as taking charge of the treasure-chamber. 100.3–4: 'gemeit' (glad, proud) is loosely joined to 'of so hard a skin'; read as the hero's pride in a skin no weapon cuts.
notes.2425.3: 2425.3: 'verlobet' read as 'forsworn': she had promised not to do what she now does.
notes.1362.3: 1363.3: 'sine stübe sam iz brünne' read as the dust flying up as if something were burning; the construction is compressed.
notes.2364.4: 2364.4: 'erbunnen' read as 'robbed us of'; the speaker is not named in these lines.

nodes.text: Adventure of the Nibelungs.
To us in old tales many wonders are told
of heroes worthy of praise, of great hardship,
of joys and festivals, of weeping and lamenting;
of bold warriors' fighting you may now hear wonders told.
In Burgundy there grew up a very noble maiden,
such that in all lands there could be none more beautiful,
named Kriemhild. She became a beautiful woman;
because of her many warriors had to lose their lives.
Three kings had her in their care, noble and mighty,
Gunther and Gernot, warriors worthy of praise,
and young Giselher, a handsome warrior.
The lady was their sister; the heroes had her in their care.
A mighty queen, Lady Ute, was their mother's name.
Their father was called Dankrat, who left them the inheritance
afterwards, at the end of his life, a man rich in courage,
who in his youth too won much great honour.
The lords were generous, of high birth by lineage,
immeasurably bold in strength, the chosen warriors.
Among the Burgundians: so their land was called.
They later did mighty wonders in Etzel's land.
At Worms on the Rhine they dwelt in their power.
Very proud knights from their lands served them
with praiseworthy honour until the time of their end.
They later died wretchedly through the hatred of two women.
and also the best warriors that have ever been told of,
strong and very bold, undaunted in fierce battles.
That was Hagen of Tronje, and also his brother,
Dankwart the bold; Ortwin of Metz;
the two margraves, Gere and Eckewart;
that the lords kept up with joy all their lives,
of that, in truth, no one could ever tell you the end.
Amid this high honour Kriemhild dreamed
that she was raising a falcon, strong, beautiful and wild,
which two eagles tore with their talons. That she had to see it—
nothing more painful could ever have happened to her in this world.
She then told the dream to her mother, Ute.
She could not interpret it any better for the good girl:
The falcon that you are raising, that is a noble man.
Unless God protects him, you must soon have lost him.
What are you telling me of a man, my very dear mother?
Without a warrior's love I will always remain.
Fair as I am, I will remain so until my death,
so that I shall never come to grief through a warrior's love.
Now do not forswear it too firmly, her mother then said.
If you are ever to be glad at heart in this world,
that comes from a man's love. You will become a beautiful woman,
if God grants you a truly good knight.
Let that talk be, my very dear lady.
It has very often been shown in many women
Because of that one man's death many a mother's child died.
Adventure of Siegfried, how he was brought up.
There grew up in the Netherlands the child of a noble king,
whose father was called Siegmund, his mother Sieglind,
in a mighty castle, well known far and wide,
down on the Rhine; it was called Xanten.
Siegfried was the name of the bold, good warrior.
He tried many kingdoms out of a valiant spirit.
Because of his bodily strength he sought out foreign lands.
Ah, what bold warriors he later found among the Burgundians!
Before the bold warrior had fully grown to manhood,
he had done such wonders with his hand
His valiant hand sought nothing but fighting;
at all times it made him well known in foreign kingdoms.
Adventure: how Siegfried came to Worms.
Seldom did any heartache trouble the lord.
He heard tidings told of how a beautiful maiden
She feared she would lose him through Gunther's men.
Then people began to make the wooing very hateful to the warrior.
Then strong Siegfried said: My very dear father,
I would always be without a noble lady's love
unless I wooed where my heart has very great love.
I am quite ready to believe, however it may have come about,
that it is the warrior who stands there so splendidly.
He is bringing new tidings here into this land.
The bold Nibelungs were slain by the hero's hand,
Schilbung and Nibelung, the mighty king's sons.
He worked mighty wonders with his great strength thereafter.
When the hero rode alone, without any help,
he found before a mountain (this I have been told for certain)
by Nibelung's hoard very many bold men,
who had been strangers to him until he came to know them there.
The hoard of Nibelung had all been carried
out of a hollow mountain. Now hear a wonder told:
how the Nibelungs' men meant to divide it.
The warrior Siegfried saw this; the hero began to wonder at it.
He came so near to them that he saw the warriors,
and the warriors [saw] him too. One of them said:
Here comes the strong Siegfried, the hero from the Netherlands.
Very strange things he met with among the Nibelungs.
Schilbung and Nibelung received the warrior well.
With one accord the noble young princes
asked him, the very bold man, to divide the treasure,
and asked him for so long that he promised them to do it.
He saw so many precious stones, as we hear tell,
that a hundred great wagons could not have carried them;
still more of the red gold from the Nibelung land.
All this bold Siegfried's hand was to divide for them.
Then they gave him Nibelung's sword as payment.
They were very ill repaid by the service
that the very bold man was to render them there.
He could not bring it to an end; then the hero was attacked by them.
He had to leave the treasure undivided.
Then the two kings' men began to fight with him.
With their father's sword, which was called Balmung,
the bold man won from them by fighting the hoard and the Nibelung land.
They had there as their friends twelve bold men,
who were as strong as giants. What could it help them?
Siegfried's hand afterwards slew them in anger,
and seven hundred warriors from the Nibelung land he subdued.
Besides this, the mighty kings: he struck them both dead.
From Alberich he then came into great danger.
He thought to avenge his lords there at once,
until he afterwards found the great strength in Siegfried.
Then the strong dwarf could not hold out against him.
Like wild lions they ran to the mountain,
where he won the cloak of invisibility from Alberich.
Then Siegfried, the very bold man, became lord of the hoard.
Those who dared to fight there all lay slain.
He then had the treasure quickly taken and carried
to where the men of Nibelung had taken it from before.
Alberich the very strong then took charge of the treasure-chamber.
He had to swear him oaths that he would serve him as his servant.
He was ready to do him every kind of service.
So spoke Hagen of Tronje: That is what he has done.
No warrior ever gained such great strength.
I know still more of him, which is known to me:
the hero's hand slew a dragon.
Then he bathed in its blood; so the bold hero has
skin so hard that no weapon has cut him since.
Now we should receive the warrior all the better,
so that we do not earn his fierce hatred.
He is so bold that one should keep him friendly.
With his courage he has done so many wonders.
Then the mighty king said: You may well be right.
Now see how like a warrior he stands, ready for the peril of battle.
with joy forever after, until their death.
With happiness the king's grief and distress had vanished.
Adventure: how Kriemhild left Worms when she journeyed to the Huns.
Let us leave the messengers riding, and I will make known to you
how the queen journeyed through the land,
to Gotelind's daughter, and such fine clothes
that she brought nothing better into Etzel's land.
Although the Nibelungs' gold had been taken from her,
all who saw her she made well-disposed to her
still, with the little wealth that she could have there.
in whatever way of life each one lived,
the king's generosity saw to it that all were given plenty.
Adventure: how Kriemhild and Etzel held their wedding in the city of Vienna.
She stayed at Traismauer until the fourth day.
All that while the dust on the road never settled;
it flew up everywhere around as if something were burning,
as King Etzel's men rode through Austria.
By then the news had also been told to the king,
and at the thought of it his sorrows vanished.
and that at all times she saw twelve kings before her,
then she thought of many a sorrow that had befallen her at home.
She thought too of many honours in the land of the Nibelungs
that she had held in her power there, and that Hagen's hand
had taken from her entirely with Siegfried's death.
You have robbed us in here of very many a gallant warrior.
He struck at Hildebrand, so that one could clearly hear
Balmung ringing, which was taken from Siegfried
by bold Hagen, there where he slew the warrior.
Then Hildebrand withstood him, who let him get away with very little.
Wolfhart's uncle swung a broad blade
This is the last day of my joys.
Alas, that no one can die of grief!
Adventure: how lord Dietrich overcame Gunther and Hagen.
Then lord Dietrich himself went to find his armour.
Master Hildebrand then helped him arm himself.
The mighty man lamented so loudly then
that the building began to resound with his voice.
The hero then regained a true man's spirit.
In fury the good warrior was then armed.
Then the very bold man was overcome by him.
Gunther the very noble began to grieve over it.
Then Dietrich bound Hagen and led him to where he found
the noble Kriemhild, and gave into her hand
the boldest warrior who ever bore a sword.
from a sharp sword that lord Dietrich bore.
Yet Gunther, for all his weariness, had defended himself admirably.
The lord was bound by Dietrich's hand,
though kings should never suffer such bonds.
He thought that if he let them stay unbound,
the two of them would let no one in the land survive.
The lord of Bern took him by the hand;
then he brought him, bound, to where he found Kriemhild.
Then her anxiety was partly taken away by his suffering.
She said: King Gunther, you are most welcome to me.
however much the very noble woman had forsworn it,
she thought: Today I shall avenge my very dear husband.
Then the queen went to where she saw Hagen.
How very angrily she spoke to the warrior:
If you will give me back what you have taken from me,
then you may come home alive to the Burgundians.
Then grim Hagen said: That talk is wholly wasted,
most noble queen. I have indeed sworn
that I will not show the hoard as long as any
of my noble lords lives, and will give it to no one.
He knew well how matters stood: they would not let him live.
How could any treachery ever be greater?
He feared that, once she had taken his life,
she would then let her brother come home to his land.
I will bring it to an end, thought the noble woman.
Then she ordered her brother's life to be taken.
His head was struck off; she carried it by the hair
before the hero of Tronje. Then he was sorely grieved.
When the despondent man saw his lord's head,
the warrior then spoke to Kriemhild:
You have brought it to an end, as you wished,
and it has turned out just as I had thought.
Now the noble king of the Burgundians is dead,
Giselher and Volker, Dankwart and Gernot.
Now no one knows of the hoard but God and I.
From you, she-devil, it shall be hidden forever.
She said: Then you have paid me back badly.
Then I will at least keep Siegfried's sword.
My dear beloved wore it when you took his life
murderously, with treachery, said the grieving woman.
She drew it from the sheath; he could not prevent it.
Then she meant to rob the warrior of his life entirely.
She raised it in her hands; she struck off his head.
King Etzel saw that; then he was sorely grieved.
Alas, said the prince, how now lies dead
at a woman's hands the very best warrior
who ever came to battle or ever bore a shield!
Enemy to him though I was, it grieves me sorely.
Then Master Hildebrand said: Truly she shall have no profit
from daring to slay him, whatever may happen to me.
Though he brought me myself into fearful danger,
yet I will avenge the death of the very bold warrior.
Hildebrand in anger leapt at Kriemhild.
He dealt the queen a fierce sweeping blow.
Indeed her dread of the warrior caused her pain.
It helped her little that she screamed so fearfully.
Then all the doomed lay dead there.
The noble woman then lay hewn to pieces.
